questions.question: A developer selects a Node.js function that builds a SQL statement by inserting a request parameter into a template string. The developer asks GitHub Copilot Chat whether the function is safe. Which change should Copilot most likely recommend?

options.text: Escape single quotes in the parameter before inserting it into the string
options.why: Manual escaping is error-prone and still builds SQL from user input. It is not the recommended fix.

options.text: Use a parameterized query that passes the value separately from the SQL text
options.why: Correct. Parameterized queries prevent user input from changing the structure of the SQL statement, which removes the SQL injection risk.

options.text: Wrap the query in a try/catch block and log any database errors
options.why: Error handling does not prevent injection. A successful injected query raises no error.

options.text: Convert the function to use async/await instead of callbacks
options.why: The asynchronous style has no effect on whether the query can be injected.

questions.explanation: String-built SQL allows SQL injection. Copilot commonly proposes a parameterized query, which the developer should then confirm with tests.

questions.question: A function retrieves a list of 300 customers and then runs one database query per customer to load their orders. A developer wants GitHub Copilot to suggest a performance improvement. Which prompt is most likely to produce a useful suggestion?

options.text: Make this faster.
options.why: The prompt gives no information about how the code runs, so Copilot can only guess.

options.text: Rewrite this in a faster programming language.
options.why: The bottleneck is the number of database round trips, not the language.

options.text: This function runs one orders query per customer for about 300 customers. Suggest a way to load all orders with fewer queries.
options.why: Correct. Describing the N+1 pattern and the data size gives Copilot the context it needs to propose a single batched query.

options.text: /clear
options.why: The /clear command starts a new conversation. It does not request a suggestion.

questions.explanation: Specific context about usage and scale leads Copilot to identify the N+1 query problem and propose batching.

questions.question: GitHub Copilot proposes a fix for a security vulnerability in a pull request. Which TWO actions should the team take to validate the fix before merging? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Add a test that fails on the original code and passes with the fix
options.why: Correct. A regression test proves that the vulnerability existed and that the change addresses it.

options.text: Rely on Copilot's post-processing filters to confirm the fix is secure
options.why: The filters check suggestions for some common insecure patterns only. They do not verify that a fix is correct or complete.

options.text: Run code scanning on the pull request and confirm the alert is resolved
options.why: Correct. Code scanning analyzes the code independently of Copilot and confirms whether the alert is closed.

options.text: Ask Copilot the same question again and accept the fix if the answer is the same
options.why: Copilot output is non-deterministic, and a repeated answer is not evidence of correctness.

questions.explanation: Copilot's security suggestions are a starting point. Tests, code scanning and human review validate them.

questions.question: A team lead states that developers can skip security review of Copilot-generated code because Copilot filters insecure code before showing suggestions. Which statement correctly describes Copilot's behavior?

options.text: Copilot blocks every suggestion that contains a known vulnerability.
options.why: Copilot does not detect every vulnerability. Its filters target some common insecure patterns.

options.text: Copilot only generates code that has passed CodeQL analysis.
options.why: Suggestions are not run through CodeQL before they appear in the editor.

options.text: Copilot never suggests insecure code to users on Copilot Business.
options.why: The plan does not change the fact that the model can produce insecure code.

options.text: Copilot checks suggestions for some common insecure patterns, but suggestions can still contain vulnerabilities and must be reviewed.
options.why: Correct. Post-processing reduces some risks, but generated code still requires review, testing and scanning.

questions.explanation: Copilot's insecure-pattern checks reduce risk but do not guarantee secure output. Human review remains required.

questions.question: A developer wants Copilot Chat to help diagnose a slow endpoint. The only available example is a production log that contains customer email addresses. What should the developer do?

options.text: Remove or replace the personal data with fake values before adding the log to the prompt
options.why: Correct. Prompts leave the editor, so personal data should be removed or replaced with sample data before sharing.

options.text: Paste the log unchanged, because Copilot Business does not retain any prompts
options.why: Some Copilot features can retain prompts for a period, and organizational policy may prohibit sharing personal data regardless of retention.

options.text: Add the log file to a content exclusion and then ask Copilot to analyze it
options.why: An excluded file is not used as context, so Copilot could not analyze it. Exclusions do not anonymize data.

options.text: Switch to a different model in the model picker before pasting the log
options.why: Changing the model does not address the privacy concern.

questions.explanation: Use fake or anonymized data in prompts. Personal data and secrets should not be shared with AI tools unnecessarily.
